issues.legal_issue: An appellate court must not reverse an acquittal when the trial court adopted a reasonable view of the evidence and the grounds for reversal do not establish that view was perverse or otherwise legally unsustainable.
material_facts: The trial court acquitted the accused after identifying concerns about the delayed receipt of the FIR by the Magistrate, irregularities in the investigation and records, inconsistencies in the eyewitness accounts, and conflicts between the eyewitness accounts and the medical evidence.
The FIR, said to have been lodged shortly after midnight, reached the Magistrate several days later, and the prosecution did not satisfactorily explain the delay.
The High Court reversed the acquittal, relying in part on explanations and possibilities that were not supported by evidence.
The Supreme Court considered the trial court's view reasonable in light of the record and held that the High Court had not shown it to be perverse.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was not justified in reversing the acquittal. Its judgment was set aside and the trial court's acquittal restored.
issues.legal_principle: An appellate court may examine the entire record in an appeal against acquittal, including whether the trial court ignored admissible evidence, relied on inadmissible evidence, or wrongly placed the burden of proof. But where two views of the evidence are reasonably possible, the appellate court must not substitute its preferred view unless the acquittal is perverse or otherwise legally unsustainable. The court relied on Balak Ram v. State of U.P., Shambhoo Missir v. State of Bihar, Shailendra Pratap v. State of U.P., Narendra Singh v. State of M.P., and Ranjitsing Brahmajeetsing Sharma v. State of Maharashtra. It also applied the principles in Section 157 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and Article 21 of the Constitution concerning prompt transmission of the FIR as a safeguard: unexplained delay in its receipt by the Magistrate may support an inference that the FIR was not recorded when claimed, assessed with the other evidence and external checks. The court relied on Meharaj Singh v. State of U.P. and noted its application in Thanedar Singh v. State of M.P., Rajeevan v. State of Kerala, and Bijoy Singh v. State of Bihar, as well as the fact-specific distinction in Rajesh v. State of Gujarat. It also referred to the applicable police regulations and Section 44 of the Police Act, 1861, concerning the recording and maintenance of police records.

rule.if: appeal_against_acquittal and trial_view_reasonable and record_supports_two_views and (material_prosecution_irregularities or appellate_reasons_unsupported_by_evidence)

predicates.appeal_against_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal seeking reversal of a trial court's acquittal.
predicates.trial_view_reasonable: The trial court reached a view of the evidence that is reasonably open on the record.
predicates.record_supports_two_views: The evidence on the record reasonably permits more than one view of the accused's guilt or participation.
predicates.material_prosecution_irregularities: The prosecution record contains material irregularities or evidentiary conflicts that the trial court relied on in assessing the case.
predicates.appellate_reasons_unsupported_by_evidenc: The appellate court's reasons for rejecting the trial court's view depend on possibilities or explanations not supported by evidence.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an acquittal and the trial court's reasonable view is supported by a record permitting two views, material prosecution irregularities or unsupported appellate reasons mean the appellate court must not reverse the acquittal.
